summary: Proposes four optional cryptographic suites for IPsec that match the United States National Security Agency's Suite B specifications, in the style of the suites in RFC 4308. This memo is historic and was replaced by RFC 6379.

plainLanguage.summary: Governments like a fixed menu of secret-code recipes. This note offers four ready-made menu choices for secure connections. It is old now and has been replaced by a newer note.

questions: what are suite b cryptographic suites for ipsec
what is suite b for ipsec
subtitle: Four pre-configured sets of encryption and authentication algorithms for IPsec aligned with NSA standards.

tldr.problem: IPsec administrators have many choices of encryption and authentication algorithms and parameters. Choosing the right combination manually is complex and error-prone.
tldr.mechanism: Suite B defines four pre-validated cryptographic suites for IPsec, each with specific algorithms for ESP (data encryption) and key exchange, ranging from 128-bit to 256-bit strength, and matching the U.S. National Security Agency's approved specifications.
tldr.outcome: IPsec implementations can refer to a suite by a single name (such as 'Suite-B-GCM-256') instead of listing every algorithm individually, reducing configuration errors and improving interoperability for government and high-security deployments.

today: RFC 4869 is Historic and was replaced by RFC 6379, which updated the Suite B specifications for IPsec with newer algorithm recommendations reflecting changes in threat assessment and NSA policy.

sections.title: Cryptographic Suites and UI Suites
sections.content:
IPsec—the Internet Protocol Security protocol used for virtual private networks (VPNs) and secure site-to-site communication—allows administrators to choose individual algorithms for encrypting data, authenticating it, and exchanging keys. However, choosing the right combination is non-trivial: the algorithms must be compatible, the key strengths must match, and the choices should reflect current security best practices.

A UI suite (user interface suite) is a named collection of algorithm choices for IPsec. Rather than specifying each algorithm individually, an administrator can select a suite by name. RFC 4308 introduced two VPN suites; this RFC adds four new suites aligned with the U.S. National Security Agency's Suite B cryptography specifications, which are used by the U.S. Government to protect classified and sensitive information.
sections.plainLanguage: IPsec has many knobs and dials for secret codes. These suites let you pick all the dials at once by choosing a name instead of fiddling with each one.

sections.title: GCM Suites: Encryption and Authentication
sections.content:
The two GCM suites provide both confidentiality (encryption) and integrity (authentication) in a single operation using AES (Advanced Encryption Standard) in GCM (Galois/Counter Mode).

Suite-B-GCM-128 uses 128-bit AES-GCM for ESP and 256-bit HMAC-SHA-256 for key derivation. It specifies 256-bit elliptic-curve Diffie-Hellman (ECP) for key exchange in IKEv1 and both IKEv1 and IKEv2. Suite-B-GCM-256 is the same but with 256-bit AES-GCM, 384-bit HMAC-SHA-384, and 384-bit ECP groups, providing stronger security. Both suites mandate support for rekeying (refreshing session keys periodically).

Administrators use these suites when they need both encryption and authentication, which covers most VPN scenarios.
sections.plainLanguage: These two suites scramble your messages and also verify they haven't been tampered with. The '128' uses weaker codes, the '256' uses stronger ones.

sections.title: GMAC Suites: Authentication Only
sections.content:
The two GMAC suites provide integrity protection using AES in GMAC (Galois Message Authentication Code) mode, but do not encrypt the data. These are used only when the data is either already encrypted by the application or when encryption is not needed.

Suite-B-GMAC-128 and Suite-B-GMAC-256 mirror the GCM suites in key strength (128-bit and 256-bit respectively) and use the same key exchange and authentication specifications. The difference is that ESP uses NULL encryption (no encryption) with GMAC integrity, whereas the GCM suites add GCM encryption on top of the authentication.
sections.plainLanguage: These two suites check that messages haven't been tampered with, but don't scramble them. Use these when you do not need encryption.

sections.title: Security and Interoperability
sections.content:
Suite B suites inherit the security properties of the underlying IPsec protocols (ESP, IKEv1, IKEv2) and the algorithms specified in the normative references. The RFC notes that all implementations using these suites MUST support pre-shared key authentication in IKEv1 for interoperability, and MUST support rekeying of IPsec sessions.

The RFC warns that algorithm strengths believed secure at the time of publication may later be found weaker. Use of Suite B is restricted to organizations whose policy permits it (primarily U.S. Government agencies); other organizations should evaluate whether these suites meet their own security and performance needs.
sections.plainLanguage: These recipes work because the math inside is hard to break, but nothing is perfect forever. People who use these must follow the rules and test that their systems can talk to each other.
